About the project

A detective tool for Earth's changing climate

NASA's challenge: build a tool that selects Earth science variables, shows how they change over time, and works out what is changing, where, how much, and whether the change is significant. We built it for students and the public, and tested it on the country we live in.

Built by Team Florensiza (Bishrel) at the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, Ulaanbaatar local event.

Python · Streamlit · Plotly · SciPy · NASA POWER API. Open source under the MIT License.

🧭

What is changing?

A scanner tests 14 variables at once and ranks them by strength of evidence.

🗺️

Where?

A trend map of 587 grid cells across Mongolia, plus any point on Earth.

📈

How much?

Change per decade and in total, with a 95% confidence band on every chart.

🧪

Is it significant?

t-test and Mann-Kendall test. "Significant" only when both agree.

Why Mongolia

When the climate shifts, herders feel it first

Mongolia's economy and culture depend on livestock grazing open pasture. A dry summer followed by a harsh winter, called a dzud, can wipe out herds. Knowing which changes are real, and where, matters.

3.5 million

Source: Mongolia Dzud Response Plan 2024 (UN OCHA)

How it works

Four steps from question to verdict

STEP 1

Choose what to investigate

14 NASA variables in three themes: temperature; water; and air & energy. Each one has a simple definition and a note on why it matters. Or start with one of six guided missions.

STEP 2

Choose where

Any point on Earth, five Mongolian regions, or all of Mongolia averaged from 587 grid cells. Click any cell on the map to see its own story.

STEP 3

Choose when

The whole year or one season, any years from 1981 to 2025. Seasons often tell different stories: Mongolian summers warm while winters don't.

STEP 4

Get a verdict, with its uncertainty shown

A t-test with a 95% confidence interval, the Mann-Kendall test and Sen's slope. The app calls a trend significant only when both tests agree, explains it in plain words, and flags its limits: data-source changes, correlated years and testing many things at once.

per decade, Mongolia average. Significant (Mann-Kendall p = 0.005).

62%

of Mongolia's area warming significantly; 55% after correcting for testing 587 grid cells at once. 0% cooling.

-0.04 m/s

per decade: wind is slowing on average across Mongolia (significant), but not everywhere: at Lake Khuvsgul it is rising.

The twist

…but not evenly

Summers warm significantly at 3 of 5 Mongolian sites.

Winters lean colder (-0.17 °C per decade), but not significantly.

Meanwhile Svalbard winters (one Arctic grid point) warm +1.39 °C per decade: one variable, opposite directions. Whether they are connected ("warm Arctic, cold continent") is a debated idea to test, not proof.

Example use cases

Each mission sets up the app, asks a question and lets students guess before they see the evidence. Teachers can share any of them with a single link.
